findings.title: Cleanup progress logged at Error level, including full ID slices, on every batch
findings.body: The new batched cleanup logs routine progress at Error level in six places (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579): "Annotations to clean by time", "cleaned annotations by time", "Annotations to clean by count", "cleaned annotations by count", "Tags to clean", and "cleaned tags". These fire unconditionally for every batch of every annotation type on every cleanup run — including steady-state runs where count is 0 and nothing was deleted — and each line embeds the complete "ids" slice, whose length is the configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize (the PR's own test uses 32767, so a single log line can contain tens of thousands of IDs). The cleanup job also now runs every minute (see cleanup.go), so this produces a constant stream of multi-kilobyte Error log lines, which will swamp error logs and trip any alerting based on error-level log volume. Lines 534/554/576 also log "err", err where err is nil by construction. These look like debugging leftovers; they should be demoted to Debug (and the ids/cond fields dropped or truncated) before merging.

findings.title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, affecting all cleanup jobs
findings.body: The diff changes the CleanUpService ticker from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This is unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (splitting the annotation cleanup DELETE to avoid MySQL deadlocks) and is not mentioned in the description. It makes every cleanup job run 10x more often — temp file cleanup, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, and query history (the last of which runs several DELETE/count queries each cycle) — multiplying background database and filesystem load for all Grafana instances. If the intent was to let the batched annotation cleanup converge faster, that should be scoped to the annotation job or justified in the PR; otherwise this line looks like a local-testing leftover that should be reverted.

findings.title: Inline ID list for SQLite built with O(n^2) string concatenation
findings.body: In deleteByIDs, the SQLite fallback path (used when AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999) builds the IN-list string with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside a loop over all ids. Each iteration reallocates and copies the entire accumulated string, so building a list of N IDs costs O(N^2) in bytes copied — with the batch size of 32767 exercised by the new test that is on the order of several GB of copying per batch, and the tag cleanup runs the same path with even more IDs. This runs on every cleanup cycle when a large batch size is configured. Using a strings.Builder (or strings.Join on a pre-converted []string) with strconv.AppendInt would make it linear.

findings.title: Subtest cleanup registered after data creation; a failure leaves dirty tables and cascades via PK conflicts
findings.body: In TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp, each subtest creates its annotations and runs assertions (which use require, aborting the subtest on failure) before registering t.Cleanup at line 120. Because createTestAnnotations now inserts rows with explicit primary keys (ID: int64(i+1), line 241) and all subtests share the same fakeSQL database, any failure before the cleanup is registered leaves rows behind, and every subsequent subtest then fails with primary-key conflicts on IDs 1..N rather than its actual assertion result, making the real failure hard to diagnose. Registering the t.Cleanup before createTestAnnotations (so tables are truncated even on early failure) avoids the cascade.
